title.narrative: HappyTap - Building a market system for hygiene that service low-income communities | Placing the stepping stones from B2B to C

description.narrative:
HappyTap exists to address an enormous public health issue. Inadequate handwashing is a stubborn, persistent problem. It's not due to a lack of awareness by the people who need to wash hands. Nor is it cost, technology issues, or uncertainty about health impacts. Instead, it's primarily due to a lack of access to desirable and conveniently-located handwashing facilities.
HappyTap advocates for a [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jQJxddw4uYM&t=51s]new normal[/url] in hand hygiene, where facilities are always within reach—even outside the toilet. We work with diverse stakeholders to create viable, sustainable markets for hygiene facilities.

title.narrative: S4.2- Please indicate what interventions and/or facilities the program has provided to cater for 1) Hygiene and Menstrual Hygiene Management and 2) People with disabilities and 3) Gender: women and girl safety?

description.narrative:
Provide a short summary of the facilities or interventions currently provided on the following 3 topics.
1) Hygiene education and Menstrual Hygiene management. (e.g washrooms, MHM facilities, education, cleaning schedules etc)
2) In what way does the solution take people with disabilities into account. Especially toilets need to be accessible for people with disabilities.
3) How does the program currently integrate gender elements into the program. Focus on women and girl participation, privacy and safety elements

actual.value:
1) We made substantial progress in finding ways to increase ownership and maintenance of the new facilities when implemented in institutional settings (schools). It's not from training, but in using a demand-driven approach and working only with schools that 'put up their hands'. Albeit there is demand creation work in the form of advocacy. More broadly in the community, we started the ‘Hygiene Model Village’ approach, which involved working closely with local government officials and then amplifying success to create hype and recognition of the leader in the presence of their colleagues from nearby localities.
2) The portability of portable handwashing stations and the low-touch levers on the taps meant that disability access was actually a big strength of the product. We often promoted the fact that elderly people and people with limited mobility can benefit from portable stations.
3) We identified four key objectives in our most recently updated gender strategy and made notable progress.
A. To maintain a high standard of gender equity internally: in our recruitment; in our internal communications; and in our team culture. Team members report largely positive feedback on the question of internal promotion of gender equity, noting that HappyTap is trying to practice what we say in our strategy about creating the space for—and encouraging—gender equity and women’s empowerment.
B. To not exacerbate gendered differences through our marketing-communications nor in other external interactions (do no harm). We are deliberate and intentional with our external messaging to ensure that we do not—directly or indirectly through partnerships—reinforce gendered norms or stereotypes that are inconsistent with equity and empowerment. This includes our field-based promotions, in-person events, social media and other digital communications; and to the extent possible, public relations and news media.
C. To select partners and to engage with them in ways that advance the values of gender equity. During the project, HappyTap refined its due diligence process in order to be confident that gender equity and women’s empowerment is adequately reflected in the values and operational conduct of our potential partners. Our engagement with such partners to develop their own communications and messaging related to hand hygiene gave HappyTap a chance to influence the content and delivery mechanism to be positive from a gender perspective.
